title: Postgres 16 ignores my partial index when the status comes in as a bind parameter
content:
I have a 14M row `events` table and almost every query only touches pending rows, so I built a partial index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_pending_idx ON events (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
```

Run from psql with the literal inlined, the plan is an `Index Scan using events_pending_idx` in 3 ms. The same query issued by the application as a prepared statement goes back to a sequential scan:

```sql
PREPARE p(text) AS
  SELECT id FROM events
  WHERE status = $1 AND created_at > now() - interval '1 day'
  ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100;
EXPLAIN EXECUTE p('pending');
-- Seq Scan on events  (cost=0.00..421903.00 rows=98 width=8)
--   Filter: ((created_at > ...) AND (status = $1))
```

I ran `ANALYZE events` and bumped the statistics target on `status` with no change. Is the planner simply unable to prove `$1 = 'pending'` matches the index predicate, and is a full index on `(status, created_at)` the only way out?

title: deadlock detected between two transactions that update the same two rows in reverse order
content:
Two API requests transfer credits between the same pair of accounts in opposite directions and roughly one in fifty fails. Both transactions do the same thing:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
```

The second one runs with the ids swapped. Postgres 16 logs:

```
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 4711 waits for ShareLock on transaction 90124; blocked by process 4712.
         Process 4712 waits for ShareLock on transaction 90118; blocked by process 4711.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
```

I already tried wrapping the whole thing in `SERIALIZABLE`, which just turns the deadlock into a serialization failure. Is ordering the updates by `id` inside the transaction the accepted fix, or should I be taking an explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on both rows first?

title: GIN index on jsonb is skipped when I filter with ->> instead of the @> operator
content:
I store API payloads in a `jsonb` column and indexed it on Postgres 16:

```sql
CREATE INDEX docs_payload_idx ON docs USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
```

`SELECT * FROM docs WHERE payload @> '{"status":"active"}'` uses the index. The query my ORM generates does not:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id FROM docs WHERE payload ->> 'status' = 'active';
-- Seq Scan on docs  (rows=1204 width=8) (actual time=0.03..2180.4 rows=51 loops=1)
--   Filter: ((payload ->> 'status'::text) = 'active'::text)
```

I understand `jsonb_path_ops` only supports containment, but switching to the default `jsonb_ops` did not help the `->>` form either. Do I need a separate expression index like `CREATE INDEX ON docs ((payload ->> 'status'))`, or is there a way to make the planner rewrite `->>` into a containment check?

title: Timestamps shift by two hours after I changed a column from timestamptz to timestamp
content:
A reporting table on Postgres 16 stored `created_at timestamptz`. To stop the driver from converting values I changed it:

```sql
ALTER TABLE reports ALTER COLUMN created_at TYPE timestamp;
```

Every existing row now reads two hours earlier than what the application originally wrote. The server runs with `TimeZone = 'Europe/Warsaw'`:

```sql
SELECT created_at FROM reports WHERE id = 12;
-- before: 2026-03-04 14:00:00+01
-- after:  2026-03-04 13:00:00
```

I expected the cast to keep the instant and simply drop the offset. Is the `ALTER` applying the session time zone during the conversion, and can I restore the original values without a backup, e.g. by casting back with an explicit `AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'`?

title: Prisma 6 behind PgBouncer in transaction mode: prepared statement s0 already exists
content:
Prisma 6 talks to Postgres 16 through PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. Simple queries work, but under any concurrency the app starts throwing:

```bash
PrismaClientUnknownRequestError:
Error occurred during query execution:
ConnectorError { code: "42P05", message: "prepared statement \"s0\" already exists" }
```

The connection string is:

```bash
DATABASE_URL="postgresql://app:***@pgbouncer:6432/app?connection_limit=10"
```

Lowering `connection_limit` to 1 makes the error go away, which is obviously not an option in production. I know PgBouncer hands a different server connection to each transaction, so a prepared statement created on one is missing on the next. Is `?pgbouncer=true` on the URL enough on Prisma 6, or do I also need a direct connection for migrations?

title: MySQL 8 deadlocks on concurrent INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE with two unique keys
content:
I upsert page view counters from several workers into an InnoDB table that has two unique keys:

```sql
CREATE TABLE views (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  page_id INT NOT NULL,
  day DATE NOT NULL,
  hits INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_page_day (page_id, day),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_slug (slug)
);

INSERT INTO views (page_id, day, slug, hits) VALUES (?, ?, ?, 1)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE hits = hits + 1;
```

With four workers I get `ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction` a few times a minute. `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` shows both transactions holding an exclusive lock on one unique index and waiting on the other. Isolation is the default `REPEATABLE READ`. Is the second unique key the actual cause here, and does dropping it (or switching to `READ COMMITTED`) remove the deadlock, or do I just have to retry?

title: Specified key was too long: max key length is 3072 bytes when Hibernate creates a unique index
Query works on MySQL 5.7 but fails on 8.0 with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY on a selected column
content:
After moving from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0 this reporting query stopped working:

```sql
SELECT o.customer_id, c.name, SUM(o.total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
```

MySQL 8 answers:

```bash
ERROR 1055 (42000): Expression #2 of SELECT list is not in GROUP BY clause and
contains nonaggregated column 'shop.c.name' which is not functionally dependent
on columns in GROUP BY clause
```

`c.name` is unique per `c.id` so the value is never ambiguous, but `id` is not what I grouped by. I know I can remove `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` from `sql_mode`, but I would rather fix the query. Is adding `c.name` to `GROUP BY` the right fix, or should I group by `c.id` so the functional dependency is visible to the optimizer?

title: Read replica returns the previous version of a row immediately after the write on MySQL 8
content:
We write to the primary and read from a MySQL 8 replica. A POST that creates an order redirects to a page that reads the order back, and maybe one request in twenty renders the old state or a 404. `SHOW REPLICA STATUS` reports:

```bash
Seconds_Behind_Source: 0
Replica_SQL_Running_State: Waiting for dependent transaction to commit
```

so the lag is small but clearly not zero at the moment of the read. Replication is row-based with `sync_binlog=1`.

I do not want to route every read to the primary. Is `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET()` with the GTID captured after the write the standard way to make one specific read wait for the replica to catch up, or is that going to serialize the whole request?

title: E11000 duplicate key error on a unique index when the second document omits the field
content:
MongoDB 8, collection `users` with a unique index on an optional field:

```javascript
db.users.createIndex({ referralCode: 1 }, { unique: true });
```

Most users have no referral code, so the field is simply absent. The second such insert fails:

```bash
MongoServerError: E11000 duplicate key error collection: app.users
index: referralCode_1 dup key: { referralCode: null }
```

I expected a missing field to be ignored by the index. Apparently the index stores `null` for every document without the field, so only one of them can exist. Is a partial index the accepted fix here, and does `{ referralCode: { $exists: true } }` as `partialFilterExpression` still guarantee uniqueness for the documents that do have a code?

title: MongoDB 8 $lookup does not use the index on the foreign field and the pipeline takes 40s
MongoDB 8 transaction aborts with WriteConflict when two sessions update the same document
$unwind drops documents with an empty array so my $group counts are too low
Redis 7.4 answers OOM command not allowed when used memory is above maxmemory
content:
A cache instance with `maxmemory 2gb` started refusing writes:

```bash
127.0.0.1:6379> SET session:9f1 "..."
(error) OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.
```

Every key I write has a TTL, so I assumed memory would come back on its own. `INFO memory` says:

```bash
used_memory_human:2.04G
used_memory_rss_human:2.61G
maxmemory_policy:noeviction
mem_fragmentation_ratio:1.28
```

`DBSIZE` is 4.1M keys and `SCAN` with `TTL` shows most of them do expire eventually. Is `noeviction` the whole problem here, and if I switch to `allkeys-lru` do I still need to worry about the fragmentation ratio, or is `activedefrag` a separate issue?

title: Redis cache serves a stale row after an update: delete-after-write still loses the race
SCAN returns the same key twice and misses keys that were added during the iteration
ERR Can't execute get: only (P|S)SUBSCRIBE / (P|S)UNSUBSCRIBE / PING / QUIT are allowed
content:
I use one Redis 7.4 client for both pub/sub and normal reads:

```javascript
const redis = createClient();
await redis.connect();
await redis.subscribe("jobs", (msg) => console.log(msg));
const cached = await redis.get("stats:today"); // throws
```

The `GET` fails with:

```bash
ErrorReply: ERR Can't execute 'get': only (P|S)SUBSCRIBE / (P|S)UNSUBSCRIBE /
PING / QUIT / RESET are allowed in this context
```

So a connection in subscriber mode cannot run regular commands. I would rather not pay for two connections per worker. Is `duplicate()` on the client the standard pattern, or does RESP3 let a single connection handle push messages and normal replies at the same time?

title: SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked in WAL mode even though only one process writes
content:
A Python service on SQLite 3.45 in WAL mode fails intermittently:

```python
con = sqlite3.connect("app.db", timeout=5)
con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")
con.execute("BEGIN")
con.execute("UPDATE jobs SET state='running' WHERE id=?", (job_id,))
con.commit()  # sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked
```

There is one writer process, but several reader threads share the same file and one of them holds a long `SELECT` over a 400k row table while paging results.

I expected WAL to let readers and a writer coexist. Is the long-running read transaction preventing the WAL checkpoint and thus the commit, and does `PRAGMA busy_timeout` help here, or do I have to make readers finish their transactions explicitly?

title: SQLite date range query on a TEXT column returns rows outside the range
SQLite deletes a parent row even though the child table has a REFERENCES clause
DataLoader still issues one query per row: batching never happens in my resolver
Cannot return null for non-nullable field User.email although the row has an email
Abstract type SearchResult must resolve to an Object type at runtime for field Query.search
content:
I added a union:

```
union SearchResult = Post | User
type Query { search(term: String!): [SearchResult!]! }
```

The resolver returns plain rows from two tables and the request fails with:

```json
{ "errors": [{ "message": "Abstract type \"SearchResult\" must resolve to an Object type at runtime for field \"Query.search\". Either the \"SearchResult\" type should provide a \"resolveType\" function or each possible type should provide an \"isTypeOf\" function." }] }
```

The rows have no discriminator field, they are just `{ id, title }` and `{ id, email }`. Adding `__typename` to the objects I return does not seem to be picked up either.

Do I have to implement `SearchResult: { __resolveType(obj) { ... } }` in the resolver map, and is inspecting fields the only way to discriminate, or should I tag the rows in the data layer?

title: Firestore rules deny a read on a subcollection although the parent document allows it
FAILED_PRECONDITION: the query requires an index for a where plus orderBy on another field
content:
This Firestore query fails at runtime:

```javascript
const q = query(
  collection(db, "tickets"),
  where("status", "==", "open"),
  orderBy("createdAt", "desc"),
  limit(20)
);
```

with:

```bash
FirebaseError: The query requires an index. You can create it here:
https://console.firebase.google.com/... (code: failed-precondition)
```

The same query without `orderBy` works, and ordering by `status` works too. Single-field indexes exist automatically for both fields, so I assumed the combination would be handled as well.

Is a composite index mandatory whenever an equality filter and an ordering touch different fields, and does the field order in the composite index have to be `status` then `createdAt` or does it not matter?

title: onSnapshot fires twice for one write and the first snapshot has a null server timestamp
new row violates row-level security policy for table profiles on insert from the client
content:
RLS is enabled on `profiles` and this policy exists:

```sql
CREATE POLICY "own profile" ON profiles
  FOR SELECT USING (auth.uid() = user_id);
```

Selecting works. Inserting from the browser with the anon key fails:

```bash
{ code: "42501",
  message: "new row violates row-level security policy for table \"profiles\"" }
```

The same insert with the service role key succeeds, which tells me RLS is the blocker rather than the payload. The client is authenticated: `supabase.auth.getUser()` returns a user, and `user_id` in the payload equals that id.

Do I need a separate `FOR INSERT ... WITH CHECK (auth.uid() = user_id)` policy, since a `USING` clause on a SELECT policy does not apply to inserts at all?

title: Supabase realtime delivers INSERT events but old_record is empty on UPDATE and DELETE
content:
I subscribe to a table and receive events, but the payload is incomplete:

```javascript
supabase.channel("todos")
  .on("postgres_changes", { event: "*", schema: "public", table: "todos" },
      (payload) => console.log(payload.eventType, payload.old, payload.new))
  .subscribe();
```

On INSERT I get the full new row. On UPDATE, `payload.old` is `{ id: 42 }`. On DELETE it is `{ id: 42 }` as well, with no other columns.

I need the previous values to diff them client side. The table is in the `supabase_realtime` publication, otherwise nothing would arrive at all.

Is this the default `REPLICA IDENTITY` only shipping the primary key, and is `ALTER TABLE todos REPLICA IDENTITY FULL` the supported fix on Supabase, or does that break RLS filtering on realtime?

title: Supabase storage signed URL returns 403 for a bucket that works with the service role key
Prisma 6 interactive transaction fails with P2028 Transaction already closed after 5s
prisma migrate deploy stops with P3009: migrate found failed migrations in the database
content:
A migration failed halfway on staging (a `NOT NULL` column added to a table that had nulls). Every subsequent deploy now aborts before doing anything:

```bash
Error: P3009
migrate found failed migrations in the target database, new migrations
will not be applied.
The `20260114093012_add_required_slug` migration started at ... failed
```

The database is in a mixed state: the column exists but is nullable, because the `ALTER` ran and the backfill did not.

`_prisma_migrations` has the row with `finished_at = NULL` and `rolled_back_at = NULL`. Should I fix the schema by hand and then run `prisma migrate resolve --applied`, or `--rolled-back` and re-apply a corrected migration? I want to understand which one leaves the history consistent for the other environments.

title: Prisma upsert throws P2002 unique constraint failed under concurrent requests
content:
Two requests for the same user arrive at the same time and one of them fails:

```typescript
await prisma.profile.upsert({
  where: { userId },
  create: { userId, views: 1 },
  update: { views: { increment: 1 } },
});
```

```bash
PrismaClientKnownRequestError: Unique constraint failed on the fields: (`userId`)
(code: P2002)
```

`userId` has `@unique` in the schema:

```
model Profile {
  id     Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  userId Int    @unique
  views  Int    @default(0)
}
```

As far as I can tell `upsert` is a `SELECT` followed by `INSERT` or `UPDATE`, so two requests can both decide to insert. Does Prisma 6 emit a native `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` for this case on Postgres, and if not, is catching P2002 and retrying the accepted pattern?

title: Errors thrown in an async Express route never reach my error-handling middleware
ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT after calling next() and res.json() in the same middleware
req.body is undefined in a POST route although the client sends application/json
DRF serializer runs one query per row for a reverse FK despite prefetch_related
content:
Django 5.1 with DRF. The list endpoint issues 1 + N queries:

```python
class AuthorSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    recent_books = serializers.SerializerMethodField()

    def get_recent_books(self, obj):
        return [b.title for b in obj.books.filter(published=True)[:3]]

class AuthorViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    queryset = Author.objects.prefetch_related("books")
    serializer_class = AuthorSerializer
```

django-debug-toolbar shows 1 query for authors and 100 for books, so the prefetch is not being used at all.

I think calling `.filter()` on the prefetched manager discards the cache and re-queries. Is `Prefetch("books", queryset=Book.objects.filter(published=True), to_attr="published_books")` the right way to keep the filter and the prefetch, and how do I get only three per author without a per-row query?

title: RuntimeWarning: DateTimeField received a naive datetime while time zone support is active
content:
Django 5.1 with `USE_TZ = True` and `TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Warsaw"`. This code warns on every run:

```python
from datetime import datetime
Report.objects.filter(created_at__lt=datetime(2026, 1, 1))
```

```bash
RuntimeWarning: DateTimeField Report.created_at received a naive datetime
(2026-01-01 00:00:00) while time zone support is active.
```

The results are also off by an hour compared to what I see in the admin, which I assume is the naive value being interpreted as UTC.

Is `django.utils.timezone.make_aware` the right call here, or should I build the value with `timezone.now()` arithmetic? I also want to know whether `__date` lookups apply the current time zone or UTC, because that is where my daily aggregates seem to shift.

title: Filtering twice on a reverse FK returns duplicated rows and inflates my annotate Count
content:
Django 5.1. I want authors who have both a 2025 book and a 2026 book:

```python
Author.objects.filter(books__year=2025).filter(books__year=2026).annotate(
    n=Count("books")
)
```

An author with three books shows up with `n=9`, and some authors appear more than once in the result list. The generated SQL contains two separate joins to `books`, so the counted rows are the cross product.

Chaining into one `filter(books__year=2025, books__year=2026)` is not equivalent, it matches a single book that is both years and returns nothing.

Is `Count("books", distinct=True)` enough here, or does the double join still break the semantics of the count? Is a subquery with `Exists()` per year the better shape for this?

title: Django 5.1 migration hangs on ALTER TABLE and blocks every query in production
content:
This migration ran for 40 seconds on staging and locked the whole table in production:

```python
operations = [
    migrations.AddField(
        model_name="order",
        name="channel",
        field=models.CharField(max_length=32, default="web"),
    ),
]
```

While it ran, `pg_stat_activity` showed dozens of queries in `wait_event_type = Lock` behind an `AccessExclusiveLock` on `orders` (18M rows, Postgres 16). Requests timed out.

On Postgres 16 adding a column with a constant default should be metadata only, so I suspect the real cost was something else in the same transaction, or the migration waiting to acquire the lock behind a long running read.

Is setting `lock_timeout` before the migration and retrying the accepted practice, and should the column be added as nullable first with the default backfilled separately?

title: DetachedInstanceError: Instance is not bound to a Session after returning from a helper
content:
Flask 3 with Flask-SQLAlchemy. This view raises on the last line:

```python
def load_user(uid):
    with db.session.begin():
        return db.session.get(User, uid)

@app.get("/me")
def me():
    user = load_user(session["uid"])
    return {"email": user.email, "org": user.organization.name}
```

```bash
sqlalchemy.orm.exc.DetachedInstanceError: Parent instance <User at 0x7f...>
is not bound to a Session; lazy load operation of attribute 'organization'
cannot proceed
```

`user.email` works, only the relationship fails, so the object is expired/detached and the lazy load has no session to use.

Should the helper return a plain dict instead of an ORM object, or is the fix eager loading with `selectinload(User.organization)` inside the same session block? I would like to know which one is the conventional Flask pattern.

title: Working outside of application context when I query the database from a background thread
content:
Flask 3, a request kicks off a thread that writes an audit row:

```python
@app.post("/import")
def start_import():
    threading.Thread(target=run_import, args=(request.json,)).start()
    return {"status": "started"}, 202

def run_import(payload):
    db.session.add(ImportLog(payload=payload))
    db.session.commit()
```

The thread dies with:

```bash
RuntimeError: Working outside of application context.
This typically means that you attempted to use functionality that needed
the current application. To solve this, set up an application context
with app.app_context().
```

I know `current_app` and the scoped session are bound to a context that the thread does not inherit. Wrapping the body in `with app.app_context():` removes the error, but I am not sure whether the session is then shared with the request thread or a fresh one. Which is it, and does `db.session.remove()` at the end matter here?

title: QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached, connection timed out, timeout 30.00
content:
Under moderate load (about 60 concurrent requests) a Flask 3 API starts failing:

```bash
sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError: QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached,
connection timed out, timeout 30.00 (Background on this error at:
https://sqlalche.me/e/20/3o7r)
```

Config:

```python
app.config["SQLALCHEMY_ENGINE_OPTIONS"] = {"pool_size": 5, "max_overflow": 10}
```

Postgres `max_connections` is 100 and `pg_stat_activity` shows only 15 connections from this service, all `idle in transaction`. That points at connections never being returned rather than the pool being too small.

I have one endpoint that opens a session, calls an external HTTP API and commits afterwards. Is that the leak, and is a teardown handler calling `db.session.remove()` the standard guard, or should the pool be bigger regardless?

title: Laravel 11 validation rejects a profile update with the email has already been taken
Laravel 11 Sanctum returns 419 CSRF token mismatch for a SPA on a different subdomain
content:
SPA on `app.example.test`, API on `api.example.test`, Laravel 11 with Sanctum SPA authentication. The call to `/sanctum/csrf-cookie` succeeds and sets `XSRF-TOKEN`, but the login POST fails with `419 CSRF token mismatch`.

```
// config/sanctum.php
'stateful' => explode(',', env('SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS', 'localhost')),

// .env
SESSION_DOMAIN=api.example.test
SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS=app.example.test
```

The browser does send the cookie on the login request and `withCredentials` is on.

My guess is `SESSION_DOMAIN` is scoped too narrowly, so the SPA origin cannot read the cookie back. Should it be `.example.test` with a leading dot, and does `SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS` need the port when running on a non-standard one?

title: Blade view fires 200 queries: N+1 on a nested relation that with() does not cover
LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy after the transaction commits
MultipleBagFetchException: cannot simultaneously fetch multiple bags with two join fetch
content:
Spring Boot 3.4 fails to start after I added a second `join fetch`:

```
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.lines join fetch o.payments where o.id = :id")
Optional<Order> findFullOrder(@Param("id") Long id);
```

```bash
org.hibernate.loader.MultipleBagFetchException: cannot simultaneously fetch
multiple bags: [com.example.Order.lines, com.example.Order.payments]
```

Both associations are declared as `List` without an `@OrderColumn`, so Hibernate treats them as bags and cannot tell the cartesian product apart.

Changing both to `Set` removes the exception, but then one query returns `lines.size() * payments.size()` rows over the wire. Is two separate queries in the same transaction (letting the persistence context stitch them together) the recommended shape, or does `@BatchSize` solve this without the cartesian product?

title: Rails 8 includes with a where on the association raises a missing FROM-clause entry
content:
Rails 8 with Postgres. This scope blows up:

```
Author.includes(:books).where("books.year = ?", 2026)
```

```bash
ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid: PG::UndefinedTable: ERROR:
missing FROM-clause entry for table "books"
```

If I add `.references(:books)` it works, and the log then shows one `LEFT OUTER JOIN` instead of two separate queries.

So `includes` sometimes preloads with a second query and sometimes joins, and a raw SQL condition forces the join without telling it. Is `references` always required with a string condition, and does using the hash form `where(books: { year: 2026 })` make it unnecessary? I would like to know which one to standardize on.

title: after_commit callback never runs in tests but works in development on Rails 8
content:
The model enqueues a job after commit:

```
class Order < ApplicationRecord
  after_commit :notify_warehouse, on: :create
end
```

In development the job is enqueued. In the test suite the callback is never called:

```
test "enqueues a warehouse job" do
  assert_enqueued_jobs 1 do
    Order.create!(total: 10)
  end
end
```

`assert_enqueued_jobs` fails with `0 instead of 1`. The record is created, other callbacks such as `after_save` do fire.

`use_transactional_tests` is on, so the test runs inside a transaction that never commits, which I assume is why `after_commit` is skipped. Is `self.use_transactional_tests = false` for that one test the usual answer, or is there a supported way to run the commit callbacks inside the test transaction?

title: ActiveRecord::Deadlocked when two jobs increment counter_cache on the same parent row
content:
Rails 8, Postgres 16. Two background jobs create comments on the same post and one of them dies:

```
class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :post, counter_cache: true
end
```

```bash
ActiveRecord::Deadlocked: PG::TRDeadlockDetected: ERROR: deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 8812 waits for ShareLock on transaction 55231; blocked by
process 8813.
```

Each job inserts several comments in one transaction, so both hold the `posts` row lock for the counter update and touch other rows in between.

The rate is low but nonzero and it takes a job to the dead letter queue. Should I drop `counter_cache` in favour of a periodic recount, or is ordering the inserts and moving the counter update to the very end of the transaction enough to make the lock order consistent?
